bull_bear.body:
- Company is one of few players with **more cell than module capacity** — net merchant-cell seller into a structurally short Indian cell market (cell ~31 GW vs module ~173 GW installed nameplate).

- TOPCon upgrade lifts watt-peak/cell from ~7.8 Wp to ~9.3 Wp (cell-size G12R 182×210 + efficiency) — meaningful revenue-per-cell uplift independent of price.
- Mono PERC retained deliberately — KUSUM/Surya Ghar rooftop demand still favors PERC; line-2 stays PERC for now.
- One-off earnings tailwinds (tax credits) ending in FY27 — headline growth will face a tougher base.

bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Upstream supply-chain dependence on imported polysilicon and wafers — India polysilicon and wafer requirements are still largely met through imports, exposing manufacturers to price volatility and to concentration among a small number of global suppliers. The SWOT names dependence on China for critical materials and equipment as a supply-chain and geopolitical risk, and upstream wafer and polysilicon supply is flagged as a structural weakness of the domestic ecosystem.
- Global oversupply and aggressive pricing compressing realisations and margins — Global oversupply of cells and modules and aggressive pricing, particularly from established overseas manufacturers, can compress realisations and margins. Listed as a threat in the SWOT analysis.
- Rapid technology obsolescence - Mono PERC to TOPCon and N-type transition — The pace of technological change is rapid; the transition from Mono PERC to TOPCon and other N-type technologies can shorten product life cycles and requires continued capital investment to remain competitive. Rapid technology shifts are also cited as a sector weakness requiring continuous upgrades.
- Policy dependence - timing and implementation of the ALMM cell mandate and related schemes — The Company is exposed to the timing and implementation of policy measures such as the ALMM cell mandate. The SWOT adds that policy or implementation delays can affect investment visibility. Demand for domestic cells is materially tied to ALMM List-II taking effect from 1 June 2026.
- Currency movements and input-cost inflation — Currency movements and input-cost inflation can affect project economics. The SWOT notes that energy-led inflation and a weaker rupee can raise input and financing costs, in a year in which the rupee weakened past 95 against the US dollar.
- Occupational health and safety in cell and module manufacturing — Manufacturing involves chemical treatment, metallization and electrical testing, which carry inherent safety risks; any lapse can result in workplace incidents, regulatory non-compliance, operational disruption and reputational impact. Mitigated through OHS management systems, PPE, safety training and ISO 45001 certification.
- Labour management and human rights across a labour-intensive, part-contract workforce — Cell and module manufacturing is labour-intensive with both permanent and contract workers; non-compliance with labour regulations, inadequate working conditions or workforce dissatisfaction may lead to operational disruptions, legal liabilities and reputational risk. Human rights gaps in operations or the supply chain may lead to regulatory action and loss of business, especially in export markets where human rights due diligence is increasingly mandated. Permanent employee turnover was 23% and permanent worker turnover 24% in FY 2025-26.
- Responsible supply-chain oversight across a multi-tier supplier base — Solar manufacturing relies on a multi-tier supply chain, and inadequate oversight of supplier practices is identified in the BRSR material-issues table as a risk to the Company.
- Concentration - single product line, single plant, and customer concentration — The business activity falls within a single business segment (solar PV cells and modules) run from one manufacturing plant at Falta, with 99.96% of turnover from that activity. Sales to dealers/distributors were 99.96% of total sales and the top 10 dealers/distributors accounted for 62.18% of those sales in FY 2025-26, so demand is concentrated in a small number of counterparties in one domestic market (exports were only 0.12% of turnover).
- Execution and ramp risk on the multi-gigawatt expansion roadmap — The Company is committing to a TOPCon upgrade targeted for early 2027, a greenfield project from 2027 and 2 GW integrated lines in 2027 and 2028, partly debt- and equity-funded. Management explicitly frames the phased approach as a de-risking response, noting that expansion after process stabilisation gives smoother ramp-up and that land, transmission and PPA delays can stretch project timelines in the sector.

outlook.body:
- Phased expansion philosophy - Expand with visibility. Scale with control. Capacity is added in stages aligned to market demand, execution readiness and long-term value creation rather than announced for its own sake.
- Technology-led scaling: transition manufacturing from Mono PERC to TOPCon and other N-type technologies, adopting the right technologies at the right time rather than chasing every new development.
- Financial prudence in growth - fund expansion primarily through internal accruals and controlled leverage, keeping growth aligned with financial capacity and preserving balance sheet resilience.
- Stabilise before scaling - expand only after process stabilisation, so each stage establishes a stronger base for the next and ramp-up risk is reduced.
- Focus on the domestic Indian market, where demand visibility is strong and domestic-content requirements (ALMM, DCR) are tightening in favour of integrated domestic manufacturers.
- Build integrated cell-and-module manufacturing depth - the roadmap moves from standalone cell lines toward integrated 2 GW cell-and-module lines.
- Execute the next phase of expansion through a wholly-owned subsidiary, Websol Renewables Private Limited, incorporated during FY26 for the proposed enhancement of solar cell and module manufacturing capacity.
- Operational excellence focus - improving operational efficiencies, optimising production yields, process automation and integration, and yield improvement systems.
- Continued investment in skill development and technical training for the Falta workforce as the Company transitions to TOPCon and scales capacity.
- Strengthen the local vendor and supplier ecosystem in line with the broader push towards supply-chain localisation.

outlook.body: Websol commissioned a second 600 MW solar cell manufacturing line at its Falta, West Bengal facility in September 2025, within the planned timeline and funded entirely through internal accruals, taking installed solar cell capacity to approximately 1.2 GW alongside 550 MW of solar module capacity. The Company has decided to upgrade one of its existing Mono PERC cell lines to TOPCon technology, which is expected to lift effective cell capacity to approximately 1.35 GW and raise conversion efficiency above 24.5%, with commercial production targeted for early 2027; the expansion roadmap describes this as taking that 600 MW line to 750 MW by FY27. Beyond that, the Board has finalised a major greenfield expansion project expected to be completed beginning in 2027, on completion of which total solar cell manufacturing capacity is expected to reach 3.35 GW, to be financed through a prudent combination of debt, equity and internal accruals. The MD&A roadmap sets out a first 2 GW integrated cell-and-module line targeted for 2027 followed by a further 2 GW line in 2028, on completion of which manufacturing capacity is expected to reach approximately 5.35 GW of cells and 4.55 GW of modules. During FY26 the Company also approved a phased expansion of 4 GW of solar cell and 4 GW of solar module capacity to be executed through Websol Renewables Private Limited, its wholly-owned subsidiary incorporated on 13 October 2025 for the next phase of expansion. The stated expansion philosophy is phased and disciplined - Expand with visibility, scale with control - with capital deployed progressively, capacity linked to market visibility and expansion undertaken only after process stabilisation. On the energy side, installation of a 700 kW rooftop solar power system for captive consumption was in progress at the reporting date. outlook.body:
- The ALMM List-II cell mandate effective 1 June 2026 extends the domestic content requirement to solar cells, and with enlisted cell capacity significantly below module manufacturing capacity, it has tightened the availability of compliant domestic cells - management expects domestic cells to be both mandated and in short supply.
- A structural gap between downstream module capacity (~172 GW) and upstream cell production (~27 GW) in India favours integrated and TOPCon-ready cell producers.
- India target of 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030 provides long-term demand visibility, with meeting the target expected to require investments of the order of US$200 billion in generation alone.
- Record solar additions in India - 44.6 GW added in FY26, up approximately 87% year-on-year, driven by growth across utility-scale, rooftop and commercial & industrial segments.
- Policy support through PLI, PM Surya Ghar, PM-KUSUM, ALMM and basic customs duty protection continues to accelerate deployment and domestic manufacturing.
- For the solar sector the medium-term outlook remains structurally strong - declining costs, the 500 GW target and growing emphasis on energy security continue to support sustained demand, while the ALMM cell mandate and the PLI scheme are reshaping the manufacturing landscape in favour of domestic, technologically advanced producers.
- Management flags the coming year as more finely balanced than the year just concluded: the West Asia conflict and energy prices will determine the pace at which inflation moderates, and Indian growth is expected to moderate from elevated FY26 levels as the energy shock feeds through, though underlying fundamentals remain intact.
- Margin/mix levers cited: higher capacity, improved utilisation, operational efficiencies and improved economies of scale, with firm demand for domestically manufactured cells and modules.
- Higher conversion efficiency as a commercial lever - the TOPCon upgrade is expected to increase conversion efficiency above 24.5%, and customers prioritise conversion efficiency, product reliability and bankability.
- Headwinds management names: global oversupply and aggressive pricing from established overseas manufacturers can compress realisations and margins; energy-led inflation and a weaker rupee can raise input and financing costs.
- The order book remained healthy at Rs 1,161 Crore as at 31 March 2026, providing revenue visibility for the coming quarters.
- Robust order book of Rs 1,161 Crore supporting revenue visibility, cited as an FY 2025-26 value signal for customers and EPC developers.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- The ALMM List-II cell mandate effective 1 June 2026 extends the domestic content requirement to solar cells, and with enlisted cell capacity significantly below module manufacturing capacity, it has tightened the availability of compliant domestic cells - management expects domestic cells to be both mandated and in short supply.
- A structural gap between downstream module capacity (~172 GW) and upstream cell production (~27 GW) in India favours integrated and TOPCon-ready cell producers.
- India target of 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030 provides long-term demand visibility, with meeting the target expected to require investments of the order of US$200 billion in generation alone.
- Record solar additions in India - 44.6 GW added in FY26, up approximately 87% year-on-year, driven by growth across utility-scale, rooftop and commercial & industrial segments.
- Policy support through PLI, PM Surya Ghar, PM-KUSUM, ALMM and basic customs duty protection continues to accelerate deployment and domestic manufacturing.
- For the solar sector the medium-term outlook remains structurally strong - declining costs, the 500 GW target and growing emphasis on energy security continue to support sustained demand, while the ALMM cell mandate and the PLI scheme are reshaping the manufacturing landscape in favour of domestic, technologically advanced producers.
- Management flags the coming year as more finely balanced than the year just concluded: the West Asia conflict and energy prices will determine the pace at which inflation moderates, and Indian growth is expected to moderate from elevated FY26 levels as the energy shock feeds through, though underlying fundamentals remain intact.
- Margin/mix levers cited: higher capacity, improved utilisation, operational efficiencies and improved economies of scale, with firm demand for domestically manufactured cells and modules.
- Higher conversion efficiency as a commercial lever - the TOPCon upgrade is expected to increase conversion efficiency above 24.5%, and customers prioritise conversion efficiency, product reliability and bankability.
- Headwinds management names: global oversupply and aggressive pricing from established overseas manufacturers can compress realisations and margins; energy-led inflation and a weaker rupee can raise input and financing costs.

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: Websol commissioned a second 600 MW solar cell manufacturing line at its Falta, West Bengal facility in September 2025, within the planned timeline and funded entirely through internal accruals, taking installed solar cell capacity to approximately 1.2 GW alongside 550 MW of solar module capacity. The Company has decided to upgrade one of its existing Mono PERC cell lines to TOPCon technology, which is expected to lift effective cell capacity to approximately 1.35 GW and raise conversion efficiency above 24.5%, with commercial production targeted for early 2027; the expansion roadmap describes this as taking that 600 MW line to 750 MW by FY27. Beyond that, the Board has finalised a major greenfield expansion project expected to be completed beginning in 2027, on completion of which total solar cell manufacturing capacity is expected to reach 3.35 GW, to be financed through a prudent combination of debt, equity and internal accruals. The MD&A roadmap sets out a first 2 GW integrated cell-and-module line targeted for 2027 followed by a further 2 GW line in 2028, on completion of which manufacturing capacity is expected to reach approximately 5.35 GW of cells and 4.55 GW of modules. During FY26 the Company also approved a phased expansion of 4 GW of solar cell and 4 GW of solar module capacity to be executed through Websol Renewables Private Limited, its wholly-owned subsidiary incorporated on 13 October 2025 for the next phase of expansion. The stated expansion philosophy is phased and disciplined - Expand with visibility, scale with control - with capital deployed progressively, capacity linked to market visibility and expansion undertaken only after process stabilisation. On the energy side, installation of a 700 kW rooftop solar power system for captive consumption was in progress at the reporting date. themes.title: Solar PV cell-to-module manufacturing
themes.need: Solar module/cell manufacturers ride capacity ramp, ALMM/DCR protection and an order-book build-out - a manufacturing thesis distinct from firm-power/FDRE tender economics or merchant storage arbitrage. Q1FY27 quantified the DCR arbitrage: EMMVEE grew revenue 51% to INR 1,555cr with EBITDA margin up to 35.2% and PAT +103% on a 9.9 GW order book, with DCR modules earning INR 8.5-9/W of EBITDA against INR 2-2.5/W for non-DCR - a 3-4x per-watt gap that structurally separates integrated cell makers from module assemblers. The offset is order timing: SWSOLAR booked a record INR 13,000cr unexecuted order value on a landmark USD 560m Egypt win (1,000 MW solar + 600 MWh BESS) yet revenue still fell 10% YoY, and flagged that industry orders concluded only ~INR 6,400cr against the >INR 20,000cr expected, deferred by DCR/module-price uncertainty.
themes.driver: DCR cell/module capacity commissioning and the ALMM List-2 per-watt spread; domestic ordering restarting after two slow quarters (SWSOLAR); order-book conversion.
